source_read: PDF (version of record), Int J Drug Policy 145 (2025) 104976, article pages 1–6, all read. Table 1 (p. 4, printed landscape) read from a 300-dpi render rotated upright, because the text layer is scrambled. Figure 1 (p. 3) checked at 300 dpi; the panel A medians are read from the figure. Totals, shares and Wilson bounds recomputed by script. Supplementary materials 1–2 not seen.

claims.overstatement: Wording: the source says ONS counts an opioid only when it is individually named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest (p. 1). 'The cause of death the coroner records' matches this more closely than 'the coroner's conclusion', which in England and Wales is a separate entry on that record.
claims.note: The coroner determines the final cause of death from all the evidence (p. 2), so 'coroners in England and Wales' as the deciders is supported. ONS finds substances by natural language processing of the cause-of-death text.

anchors.extracted: ONS treats a death as opioid-related only when the opioid is individually named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest. With an ambiguous cause (e.g. multi-drug toxicity, polydrug use) ONS cannot tell which substances were involved, and ONS itself says its substance-specific counts are likely underestimates.

anchors.locator: Methods › Office for national statistics data
anchors.extracted: ONS identifies specific substances in the cause-of-death fields by natural language processing and gives each a unique identifier. The data used are ONS 2023 registrations, by year the death occurred.

anchors.locator: Methods › National programme on substance use mortality data, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The coroner determines the final cause or causes of death after weighing police records, emergency-service contact, pathology, toxicology and GP summaries. The programme also receives the toxicology report, in which the consulting toxicologist assesses each detected substance's likely involvement in the death.

claims.overstatement: Not supported: 'with the programme's toxicologist implicating the opioid'. The source says the consulting toxicologist did this, in the toxicology report that the programme receives (p. 2), not a toxicologist of the programme. This matters for 'who decided'. Also, 'coroner's conclusion' should be 'the cause of death the coroner records' (p. 1). If the magnitude's closing 'No intervals for any correction' is meant to cover Chen, it is wrong: Chen prints Wilson intervals for every projected count, although these cover only the sampling error of the programme's share.
claims.note: All numbers match. 2011: 122/416 = 29.3%. 2022: 1 − 1,264/1,980 = 36.2%. Overall shares not counted, recomputed from Table 1: methadone 39.1%, tramadol 36.5%, dihydrocodeine 35.2%, codeine 34.0%, heroin/morphine 33.7%, fentanyl 32.5%, i.e. official counts held 60.9% to 67.5% (61% to 68%). 13,471 + 6,852 = 20,323. 16,101/16,628 = 96.8%. The yearly heroin/morphine share not counted ranges from 28.1% (2015) to 36.9% (2018), so 29% and 36% are endpoint years, not the extremes. The projection can only add deaths and assumes the programme's share of ambiguous causes holds for all drug deaths. The claim's 'projected' and 'without linking the records' are accurate.

anchors.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Privacy rules prevented record linkage, so the datasets were triangulated. Programme cases of 2011–2022, reported by 1 August 2024, were coded as specific opioid named (Code 1) or ambiguous drug cause (Code 2). ONS counts were then scaled up on the assumption that they represent only the named share; the paper's example is 123 of 183, i.e. 67%. 95% CIs use the Wilson score method.

anchors.locator: Methods › National programme on substance use mortality data, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The programme receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales. An opioid-related death is one where the coroner cited an opioid (by name, or as 'opioid' or 'opiate'), or gave an ambiguous drug cause and the consulting toxicologist implicated the opioid as causative. Paracetamol–opioid combinations were excluded to match ONS.

2011: ONS 574 heroin/morphine deaths. The programme had 416, of which 122 (29.3%) had ambiguous causes, giving 239 more (95% CI 193–294) and 813 in total (767–868). 2022: 36% not counted (ONS 1,264; estimated 1,980, printed here as 1,895–2,075). 2011–2022: ONS 13,471 plus a further 6,852 (6,557–7,132), 34% overall. Other opioids: methadone 39%, tramadol 36%, dihydrocodeine 35%, codeine 34%, fentanyl 32%.

anchors.locator: Table 1 (printed landscape), totals and % underestimate columns
anchors.extracted: ONS against estimated, 2011–2022: heroin/morphine 13,471 against 20,323 (19,382–21,358), 34%; methadone 5,752 against 9,444, 39%; tramadol 2,455 against 3,865, 36%; dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854, 35%; fentanyl 599 against 887, 32%; codeine 1,886 against 2,859, 34%. The yearly columns sum to the printed totals.
96.8% (16,101 of 16,628) of the programme's opioid-related deaths had more than one drug detected by post-mortem toxicology.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of this and other studies (continues on p. 4)
anchors.extracted: The programme lacks complete coverage of drug-poisoning deaths, but it has the full toxicology. The figures are estimates: there was no record linkage, and the programme's share of ambiguous causes is assumed to represent all drug deaths. Coroners' practice varies, which could bias this. Toxicology is not always comprehensive, so polydrug use may be understated.

The authors hypothesise that rising polydrug use leads coroners to use short, ambiguous terms. Other reasons they give for ambiguous causes: legal sensitivity about prescription drugs, simpler wording for families, and a focus on intent in suicides and deaths of undetermined intent.

claims.overstatement: Not supported: the magnitude's 'no intervals for the Victorian or projected counts', as far as Chen is concerned. Chen prints 95% CIs for every projected count, e.g. 813 (767–868), 1,980 (1,894–2,074), 20,323 (19,382–21,358). Better wording: the printed intervals cover only the sampling error of the programme's share, not the unlinked-projection assumption. For England and Wales, ONS and the programme count heroin and morphine together, so this evidence shows only the general-term mechanism, not morphine written instead of heroin. 'Coroner's conclusion' should be 'the cause of death the coroner records' (p. 1).
claims.note: All numbers match the rendered pages: 13,471; 29% (2011); 36% (2022); 20,323; 20,323/13,471 = 1.509 (about 51% more); 574 against 813 (767–868); 1,264 against 1,980. The median drugs detected in heroin/morphine cases were 4 in 2011 and 6 in 2022 (Figure 1A; the abstract says 'co-administered', the Results 'detected at post-mortem'). The abstract prints 765–866 for 2011, against 767–868 in the Results and Table 1; recomputing Wilson bounds on 122/416 gives 766.9–868.1. The yearly projections are close to ONS/(1 − share): 2011 gives 812.2 against the printed 813.

anchors.extracted: Heroin/morphine: 2011, ONS 574; the programme's ambiguous-cause share was 29.3% (122/416), giving 813 (767–868). 2022: ONS 1,264, estimated 1,980, 36% not counted. 2011–2022: ONS 13,471, a further 6,852 (6,557–7,132) not counted.

ONS against estimated by year, from 574 against 813 (767–868) in 2011 to 1,264 against 1,980 (1,894–2,074) in 2022; total 13,471 against 20,323 (19,382–21,358), 34%. 2015 is printed as 1,727 (1,657–2,803), an evident typographical error.

anchors.locator: Figure 1, panel A (Heroin/Morphine), orange series; Abstract (p. 1)
anchors.extracted: Median number of drugs detected after death in heroin/morphine cases: 4 in 2011, 6 in 2022 (4, 4, 5, 4, 5, 5, then 6 from 2017). The share captured by ONS falls from about 71% to about 64%. The abstract gives four and six, with ρ = 0.81 for the link between underestimation and the median.
ONS counts an opioid only when it is named individually in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest; ambiguous terms hide the substances.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of this and other studies (continues on p. 4)
anchors.extracted: No linkage. The programme's ambiguous share is assumed representative, and coroners' practice varies. Toxicology screens may miss substances. The figures are estimates.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. All first, last, minimum and maximum yearly shares recompute from Table 1 as printed in the card.

Confirmed as printed (p. 2, Results, 2nd paragraph). From Table 1 and my own readings of the Figure 1 medians, every median-with-year value and the methadone, tramadol and heroin/morphine values reproduce exactly. Dihydrocodeine's share-missed-with-year recomputes as 0.41 against the printed 0.43, within rounding.
Confirmed. 16,101/16,628 = 96.8%. Figure 1A medians at 300 dpi: 4, 4, 5, 4, 5, 5, then 6 from 2017 to 2022.

reporting_issues.note: The substance is confirmed: the five relationships are positive and codeine's is negative (−0.59). One correction: by my reading of Figure 1A (4, 4, 5, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6), heroin/morphine recomputes as 0.81, exactly the printed size, not 0.79. That reading also reproduces the printed 0.90 for median with year. Methadone 0.79, tramadol 0.78, dihydrocodeine 0.39 and fentanyl 0.33 match the card.

Recomputed: two-sided p ≈ 0.163, 0.186 and 0.295 for r = 0.43, 0.41 and 0.33 with n = 12.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with JBI-prevalence, overall high, for the projected totals. ONS's named-cause counts and the 96.8% polydrug figure are direct counts with lower risk.

interpretation_gap.note: I agree with 'substantial'. The title 'suggests' becomes 'demonstrates' in the Conclusions. Polydrug use as the cause rests on two trending 12-year series. 'Similar trends' fails for codeine. The policy consequences are untested. The tramadol 'two years beforehand' is a difference in level, as the card says (Table 1: estimates 246, 235, 329 against ONS 165, 184, 254).

missed: The projection runs in one direction only. It treats every ONS death naming an opioid as correct and adds the programme's ambiguous-cause share, so it cannot detect ONS-counted deaths that a toxicologist would not implicate, i.e. over-counting. The paper therefore measures undercounting only. This is relevant to the 'both directions' wording in cl_gen_deaths_missed.

Both sources count heroin and morphine as one category (ONS 'heroin/morphine'; Table 1; Results, p. 2). The study therefore says nothing about heroin being recorded as morphine; it shows only that ambiguous terms hide both. This is relevant to cl_opi_deaths_heroin_missed, whose opening sentence names morphine written instead of heroin as a main mechanism across all three places.

Who judged involvement in the added deaths: the consulting toxicologist, whose report the coroner commissions and the programme receives (p. 2), not a toxicologist of the programme. The card has this right (KF2). One staged claim, cl_gen_deaths_missed, says 'the programme's toxicologist'.
